holding: For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds no illegality, irregularity or jurisdictional defect in the impugned judgments and decrees of the learned courts below. Consequently, this constitutional petition is dismissed with no order as to costs.

paragraphs.text: Date of Hearing. 21.10.2026 PETITIONERS BY: Syed Fida Hussain Babar Gillani, Advocate. RESPONDENTS BY: M/s Ch. Nisar Ahmad and Shehla Parveen, Advocates for respondents No.1 and 2. Asad Ali Bajwa, J:-.Through this petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 the petitioners challenge the vires of judgment and decree dated 06.07.2026 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Gujranwala as well as judgment and decree dated 06.10.2025 passed by the learned Judge, Family Court, Gujranwala.

Brief facts of the case are that respondents No.1 and 2 filed a composite suit for recovery of maintenance allowance, dower and dowry articles against the petitioners. It was averred in the plaint that the marriage between petitioner No.1 and respondent No.1 was solemnized on 18.08.2019 in accordance with Islamic Sharia and two minors, namely Abdul Wasay and Abdul Rafay were born out of the wedlock. Respondent No.1 further stated that the relationship between the spouses initially remained cordial but subsequently petitioner No.1 expelled her from the matrimonial home along with minor respondent No.2 whereas her other son Abdul Rafay remained in the custody of his paternal grandparents. She further averred that at the time of marriage her parents gave her dowry articles worth Rs.46,73,983/-, which remained in the possession of petitioner No.1. The petitioners contested the suit by filing a written statement, raising legal as well as factual objections. As the pre-trial reconciliation proceedings failed, the learned trial Court framed issues and recorded the oral and documentary evidence produced by both parties. After considering the evidence and hearing learned counsel for the parties, the learned trial Court partially decreed the suit. Respondent No.1 was held entitled to recover maintenance allowance at the rate of Rs.12,000/- per month for the period of Iddat (amounting to Rs.36,000/- in total). She was also held entitled to recover the dowry articles mentioned in list Ex.P2 except items mentioned at serial Nos.11, 13, 14, 19, 27, 28, 35, 61, 78, 83, 86 to 90, 92, 93, 96, 103 and 105 to 202 and their alternate value was determined as Rs.9,70,000/-. Her claim regarding dower was declined. Respondent No.2 was held entitled to recover maintenance allowance at the rate of Rs.10,000/- per month from the date of institution of the suit until his legal entitlement with annual increase of 10%. Feeling aggrieved, both parties filed separate appeals. The learned Additional District Judge, Gujranwala vide consolidated judgment and decree dated 06.07.2026 dismissed the appeal filed by the petitioners and allowed the appeal filed by respondents No.1 and 2 and enhanced the maintenance allowance of minor respondent No.2 from Rs.10,000/- to Rs.25,000/- per month from the date of institution of the suit until his legal entitlement with annual increase of 10%. Hence this petition.

Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that the judgments and decrees passed by the learned Courts below are contrary to law and facts. He submits that petitioner No.1 raised concerns regarding the legitimacy of respondent No.2 and disowned his paternity. Consequently, petitioner No.1 got DNA test allegedly conducted from AlphaBio labs U.K, which returned as (paternity excluded), therefore grant of maintenance allowance in his favour is illegal, however this fact was not considered by either of the learned Courts below. He further contends that respondent No.1 failed to prove her claim regarding dowry articles yet the learned Courts below decreed the same in her favour. He maintains that the findings recorded by the learned Courts below are the result of misreading and non-reading of the evidence available on the record.

Conversely, learned counsel for respondents No.1 and 2 submits that the learned appellate Court has duly examined the evidence produced by the parties and recorded its findings on the basis of material available on record. He further contends that no jurisdictional defect, illegality or material irregularity has been pointed out in the impugned judgments and decrees that would warrant interference by this Court in its constitutional jurisdiction.

The first point for determination is whether respondent No.2 was entitled to maintenance allowance being legitimate child of petitioner No.1. It is evident from the record that the marriage between petitioner No.1 and respondent No.1 was solemnized on 18.08.2019 whereas respondent No.2 was born on 27.04.2022 meaning thereby the minor was born during subsistence of marriage between the parties. Petitioner No.1 was represented by his father Tahir Iqbal petitioner No.2 as special attorney who appeared in witness box as DW-1, however, mother of petitioner No.1 appeared as DW-2 while his maternal uncle appeared as DW-3. The said two witnesses DW-2 and DW-3 admitted in their depositions that at the time of birth of respondent No.2, the marriage between the spouses was intact. DW-1 during his cross-examination admitted that the petitioner No.1 (Osama Tahir) himself accompanied respondent No.1 to Kot Najeeb Hospital, Rural Health Centre, Haripur for delivery where the minor Abdul Wasay was born at 10:00 hours on 27.04.2022. This admission by attorney of petitioner No.1 shall be construed admission by petitioner No.1, father of minor. While DW-2 admitted during cross-examination that she also accompanied respondent No.1 while sitting on the rear seat of car and remained present in hospital at the time of delivery. Legitimacy of a minor is protected by Article 128 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 subject to the exception provided therein which reads as under:— “128. Birth during marriage conclusive proof of legitimacy: (1) The fact that any person was born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his mother and any man and not earlier than the expiration of six lunar months from the date of the marriage, or within two years after its dissolution, the mother remaining unmarried, shall be conclusive proof that he is the legitimate child of that man, unless— (a) the husband had refused, or refuses, to own the child; or (b) the child was born after the expiration of six lunar months from the date on which the woman had accepted that the period of iddat had come to an end. (2) Nothing contained in clause (1) shall apply to a non-Muslim if it is inconsistent with his faith.” The legitimacy is a status which results from certain facts, whereas legitimation is the procedure which creates a status, which does not exist before. Legitimacy of a child may be presumed where there had been continuous cohabitation of the parents during existence of marriage. Therefore, from the evidence of both the parties it can safely be presumed that the parties were living happily without any hesitation and doubt in pregnancy and petitioner No.1 along-with his mother were attending respondent No.1 at the hospital at the time of delivery of the minor son during valid marriage. The surrounding circumstances and the conduct of respondent No.1 is much relevant to ascertain the legitimacy under the relevant law. Reliance is placed on the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan reported as “Bashir and others V. Ilam Din and others”(PLD 1988 SC 8).

In the present case, though petitioner No.1 denied the paternity of respondent No.2 in his written statement but his plea was turned down by the learned trial Court vide order dated 05.04.2023. The reliance placed by learned counsel on a privately conducted DNA test is also of no significance. The said test was admittedly arranged privately by petitioner No.1 and no material has been brought on record to establish that it was conducted under the supervision or direction of a forum of competent jurisdiction. A unilateral DNA test report cannot by itself displace the conclusive presumption of legitimacy provided under Article 128 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. Even otherwise, the question relating to paternity of the minor has already been decided by both the learned courts below against the petitioner in the light of the evidence adduced by the parties. The legitimacy attached to paternity of a minor is more strict under Muslim Law. The courts are reluctant to stigmatize a child as illegitimate in absence of conclusive proof, therefore, presumption of legitimacy exists beyond any doubt particularly when legitimacy of a child is fully established from the surrounding circumstances. Reliance in this regard is placed on the cases reported as Muhammad Akhtar Hussain Pirzada v. Medical Superintendent, THQ, Hospital Lodhran and others (PLD 2025 SC 853) and Sharafat Ali Ashraf v. Additional District Judge, Bahawalpur (2008 SCMR 1707).

The role of the Court is not only to decide legal disputes but also to protect human dignity, especially where the rights of a minor are involved. When scientific tools like DNA testing are used to resolve questions of paternity, the Court must act with caution. A child may not be able to speak but still has constitutional rights such as the right to privacy, dignity, and protection from emotional harm. The law places the child's welfare above all other concerns. Even if both parents agree to a DNA test, the Court must still consider whether such a test is in the best interest of the child. The use of DNA testing in legal proceedings, particularly in matters of paternity, is a serious judicial act, not to be undertaken lightly or on mere request. It is not the availability of technology or the consent of parties that alone justifies such testing rather it is to be seen that whether its purpose serves the ends of justice. DNA test may have valued, but not at the cost of a child's mental and emotional well-being. The sample of a child without the consent of his/her mother is squarely against the principle of their right to liberty and privacy.

Right of personal dignity is a foremost component of Muslim society and recognized fundamental right under Article 14 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 which provides shield against undue encroachment upon private domains of an individual, therefore, reliance of the petitioner on the privately conducted DNA test is inconsequential. If such reports are permitted to be relied upon generally by the Courts while determining question relating to paternity of a child, this would amount to create anarchy in the society. As the DNA test was got conducted secretly by petitioner No.1, without permission of the Court and without consent of mother of the minor, this act violates the dignity and privacy of mother and the minor. Such DNA testing has raised significant concerns regarding the right to liberty and privacy as DNA test contains wealth of personal information about an individual such as a genetic pre-dispositions, familial relationships and ethnicity and its collection, storage or use may have implications of privacy rights. Conducting DNA test is used to establish paternity or other family relationships. It can also raise privacy concerns when individual is tested without his knowledge or consent. Bodily autonomy is protected by both the fundamental rights; right to liberty and privacy. Every individual has a right to control his own body, make his own decision and may refuse unwanted medical intervention without his prior consent. Unauthorized collection of samples for DNA test could be seen as violating the fundamental principles as it involves taking sample of an individual’s biological material without his consent. These fundamental rights, are subject to law and can only be interfered with if law so requires. Further, as per the command of Article 4 of the Constitution, no action detrimental to the liberty, body or reputation of a person can be taken except in accordance with law nor can a person be compelled to do what the law otherwise not require him to do. This being the constitutional mandate, any executive or judicial act taken in respect of right to liberty, privacy, body or reputation of a person must be backed by some law. A Court’s order for the DNA test for identification of genetic relationship interferes with the right to privacy and liberty and such test can only be ordered either with consent of the person concerned or without his consent if permissible under the law which requires DNA test. Reliance is placed on case reported as “Muhammad Nawaz v. Additional District and Sessions Judge and others” (PLD 2023 SC 461).

The right to liberty anchored under Article 9 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 surpasses mere immunity for corporeal detention and guarantees freedom from all arbitrary or purposeless restraints on an individual’s autonomy which are inconsistent with legislative intent. The demand of DNA testing by anyone at any stage particularly to ascertain parentage encroaches upon these rights, as genetic information contains comprehensive data concerning lineage and physical characteristics of an individual. Furthermore, both fundamental rights safeguard bodily integrity, securing an individual’s power to manage their physical self and reject unsolicited medical procedures. Reference in this regard is made to judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan reported as “Khalid Hameed v. Special Judge, Anti-Corruption Pakpattan Sharif and others” (2026 SCMR 1780) and “Laila Qayyum Vs. Fawad Qayum” (PLD 2019 SC 449).

In relation to matters concerning to paternity of a child, when the parties are Muslims, reference has to be made to the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1962, according to which a child born during subsistence of marriage between the parties is to be considered legitimate child. In case, if the father opts to challenge the paternity, he can do so within the period of maximum 40 days from birth. Reliance is placed on “Ghazala Tehsin Zohra v. Mehr Ghulam Dastgir Khan and another”(PLD 2015 SC 327). In the instant case, admittedly the minor was born on 27.04.2022, whereas the petitioner got conducted alleged DNA test on 05.09.2022, which carries no value in the eye of law, thus no illegality has been committed by the learned Courts below while discarding its credibility.

So far as the contention of the petitioners regarding enhancement of maintenance allowance is concerned, it is an admitted position that petitioner No.1 resided and worked in England. Respondent No.1 claimed that petitioner No.1 was earning Rs.12,00,000/- per month, whereas petitioner No.2 was employed in a factory and was earning Rs.70,000/- per month. On the other hand, the petitioners asserted that petitioner No.1 had gone to England for study purposes and was not earning there. Although respondent No.1 did not produce any documentary evidence regarding income of the petitioner No.1, however, petitioner No.2 admitted during cross-examination regarding stay of petitioner No.1 in the United Kingdom. Furthermore, petitioner No.3 admitted during cross-examination that petitioner No.1 used to send money from England directly into the bank account of petitioner No.2. These admissions lend support to the stance of respondent No.1 regarding stay of petitioner No.1 abroad as an earning hand. The learned appellate Court while enhancing the maintenance allowance of minor respondent No.2, duly considered the circumstances of the case and needs of the minor coupled with financial status of petitioner No.1. Petitioner No.1 has failed to establish that the enhanced amount is excessive or beyond his financial status. The determination of the appropriate quantum of maintenance involves two principal considerations i.e. the nature and extent of child’s reasonable requirements and the father’s financial means. Maintenance traditionally includes food, raiment and lodging. It includes educational cost, healthcare and other needs consistent with the natural growth and comfort of the minor. All the reasonable expenses are necessary for the physical, mental and emotional development of the child. The amount awarded should reflect the family social status ensuring the child is not deprived of opportunities for development and well-being solely due to the dissolution of marriage or any other factor. The second consideration pertains to the father’s financial capacity to maintain the child. Under the Islamic Principles, the obligation of maintenance is generally subject to certain conditions firstly the child must be in need, secondly unable to earn due to minority or incapacity, thirdly the father must possess the means to provide such maintenance. The obligation to maintain arises irrespective of the actual wealth provided the father has the capacity to earn. If father lacks the means to provide maintenance and is incapable of earing, the obligation may extend to paternal grand-father subject to his financial ability to provide support to the children. Reliance in this regard is placed upon case reported as “Muhammad Imran Baqir v. Mst. Zarnain Arzoo and others” (PLD 2026 SC 170). Consequently, enhancement of quantum of maintenance allowance by the learned appellate Court does not warrant interference by this Court in its constitutional jurisdiction.

As regards claim qua recovery of dowry articles, respondent No.1 asserted that dowry articles worth Rs.46,73,983/- were given to her at the time of marriage. On the other hand, the petitioners denied the delivery of dowry articles to respondent No.1. Although marriage of parents of respondent No.1 was dissolved, but DW-2 admitted during cross-examination that brothers of respondent No.1 were businessmen having reasonable sources of income, enabling them to provide dowry articles to their sister. The petitioners failed to produce any evidence to establish that financial status of family of respondent No.1 was such that they could not have provided dowry articles. It is well- established custom in our society that parents, irrespective of their financial means and social status always endeavor to give dowry articles to their daughters at the time of marriage. Nevertheless, claim for recovery of dowry articles must be determined on the basis of pleadings and evidence produced by the parties. In the present case, the learned trial Court did not accept the claim of respondent No.1 in its entirety rather, after appraising the evidence, excluded certain articles mentioned at the specified serial numbers in list Ex.P2 and granted relief only in respect of the remaining articles or their alternate value assessed at Rs.9,70,000/-. The partial decree reflects that the claim was examined in the light of the evidence available on record and was not accepted mechanically. Consequently, the petitioners have failed to point out any misreading or non-reading of evidence warranting interference in the concurrent findings of the learned Courts below.

The concurrent findings of fact recorded by the learned Courts below are supported by evidence on record and cannot be characterized as perverse or result of misreading or non-reading of material evidence warranting interference in exercise of constitutional jurisdiction of this Court. Reliance is placed on judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan reported and Shafqat Ali v Mst. Zaib un Nisa and others (2026 SCMR 494).

The jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution is not meant to substitute its own view for that of the competent forums merely because another view may be possible. Interference is only warranted where the impugned judgments/orders suffer from jurisdictional defect, patent illegality or material misreading/non-reading of record. No such defect has been demonstrated in the present case. Reliance in this regard is placed on a judgment of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported as M. Hamad Hassan vs. Mst. Isma Bukhari and 2 others (2023 SCMR 1434).

For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds no illegality, irregularity or jurisdictional defect in the impugned judgments and decrees of the learned courts below. Consequently, this constitutional petition is dismissed with no order as to costs. (ASAD ALI BAJWA) JUDGE Approved for reporting. JUDGE Abdul Waheed
